## Proof

We show that the set of subgroups of $F_2$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (the cardinality of the continuum).

### Upper bound: at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ subgroups

The free group $F_2$ on two generators is countable: its elements are reduced words in the alphabet $\{a, a^{-1}, b, b^{-1}\}$, and the set of all finite words over a finite alphabet is countable. Every subgroup of $F_2$ is a subset of $F_2$, so the set of subgroups injects into the power set $\mathcal{P}(F_2)$. Since $|F_2| = \aleph_0$, we have $|\mathcal{P}(F_2)| = 2^{\aleph_0}$. Hence the number of subgroups is at most $2^{\aleph_0}$.

### Lower bound: at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ subgroups

We establish the lower bound in three steps.

**Step 1: $F_2$ contains a free subgroup of countably infinite rank.**

Consider the commutator subgroup $[F_2, F_2]$, which is the kernel of the abelianization homomorphism $\pi: F_2 \to \mathbb{Z}^2$. Since $F_2 / [F_2, F_2] \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ is infinite, the subgroup $[F_2, F_2]$ has infinite index in $F_2$.

By the **Nielsen–Schreier theorem**, every subgroup of a free group is free, so $[F_2, F_2]$ is a free group. Since $F_2$ is countable, $[F_2, F_2]$ is countable, so its rank is at most $\aleph_0$. On the other hand, a subgroup of infinite index in $F_r$ (with $r \geq 2$) has infinite rank: if it had finite rank $s$, then by the Schreier index formula its index would be $(s-1)/(r-1)$, which is finite—a contradiction. Therefore $[F_2, F_2]$ is free of rank $\aleph_0$. Denote it $F_\omega$.

**Step 2: $F_\omega$ has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ subgroups.**

The abelianization map $\alpha: F_\omega \to \mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)}$ (where $\mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)} = \bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \mathbb{Z}$ is the free abelian group of countable rank, with standard basis $\{e_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$) is a surjective homomorphism. For each subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, define

$$K_S = \bigoplus_{i \in S} \mathbb{Z}\, e_i \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)}.$$

This is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)}$. If $S \neq T$, say $j \in S \setminus T$, then $e_j \in K_S$ but $e_j \notin K_T$ (elements of $K_T$ have support contained in $T$), so $K_S \neq K_T$. Thus the map $S \mapsto K_S$ injects $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ into the set of subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)}$, giving at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ subgroups.

Taking preimages under $\alpha$: for distinct subgroups $K_S \neq K_T$ of $\mathbb{Z}^{(\omega)}$, the preimages $\alpha^{-1}(K_S)$ and $\alpha^{-1}(K_T)$ are distinct subgroups of $F_\omega$ (if $x \in K_S \setminus K_T$ and $g \in F_\omega$ with $\alpha(g) = x$, then $g \in \alpha^{-1}(K_S) \setminus \alpha^{-1}(K_T)$). This yields at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct subgroups of $F_\omega$.

**Step 3: These are subgroups of $F_2$.**

Since $F_\omega = [F_2, F_2] \leq F_2$, every subgroup of $F_\omega$ is in particular a subgroup of $F_2$. Therefore $F_2$ has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ subgroups.

### Conclusion

Combining the upper and lower bounds:

$$2^{\aleph_0} \;\leq\; |\{\text{subgroups of } F_2\}| \;\leq\; 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

By the Cantor–Bernstein theorem, the cardinality of the set of subgroups of $F_2$ is exactly $\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}$.
